terms.definition: A single sugar unit that cannot be hydrolyzed into a simpler carbohydrate.
A six-carbon monosaccharide used widely as a respiratory substrate and building block.
A carbohydrate formed when two monosaccharides are joined by a glycosidic bond.
A polymer composed of many monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds.
A reaction that forms a covalent bond between molecules while releasing water.
Cleavage of a covalent bond by adding the components of water.
A covalent linkage joining one sugar residue to another group, commonly another sugar.
A plant glucose-storage polymer composed of amylose and branched amylopectin.
A highly branched glucose-storage polymer found mainly in animals and fungi.
An unbranched polymer of β-glucose whose hydrogen-bonded microfibrils strengthen plant cell walls.
A lipid formed from glycerol joined by ester bonds to three fatty acids.
A hydrocarbon chain with a terminal carboxyl group and variable chain length or unsaturation.
A fatty acid containing no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
A fatty acid containing one or more carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
An amphipathic lipid with a phosphate-containing head and two hydrophobic fatty-acid tails.
A protein monomer with amino and carboxyl groups bonded to a central carbon bearing a variable side chain.
The variable side chain that determines an amino acid’s chemical properties.
The covalent amide linkage formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and another’s amino group.
A linear chain of amino-acid residues joined by peptide bonds.
The specific linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Local backbone folding stabilized by hydrogen bonds, especially α-helices and β-pleated sheets.
The overall three-dimensional shape of one polypeptide produced by interactions among side chains and the backbone.
The arrangement and interaction of multiple polypeptide subunits in one functional protein.
A coiled secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds within the polypeptide backbone.
A sheet-like secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds between adjacent backbone segments.
A covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine side chains.
Loss of a protein’s native shape and function without necessarily breaking its peptide bonds.
A compact, generally soluble protein whose folded shape supports roles such as catalysis or transport.
An elongated, usually insoluble protein specialized for structural or mechanical functions.
A protein associated with a non-protein component required for its biological function.
A model describing membranes as mobile lipids containing a changing mosaic of proteins and other components.
Two layers of phospholipids with hydrophobic tails inward and hydrophilic heads facing surrounding water.
Having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions within the same molecule.
A protein permanently embedded in the lipid bilayer, often spanning it completely.
A protein loosely attached to a membrane surface or to another membrane protein.
An animal-membrane steroid that buffers fluidity and reduces permeability to small polar molecules.
A protein with covalently attached carbohydrate chains used in recognition, adhesion, or signaling.
A membrane lipid with an attached carbohydrate that contributes to cell recognition and membrane stability.
The property of allowing some substances to cross a membrane more readily than others.
Net movement down a concentration gradient directly through a membrane without a transport protein.
Passive movement down an electrochemical gradient through a channel or carrier protein.
A membrane protein forming a hydrophilic pore through which selected particles can pass.
A membrane protein that binds a solute and changes shape to move it across the bilayer.
Movement against an electrochemical gradient using energy and a specific membrane protein.
Bulk entry into a cell by invagination of the plasma membrane and formation of a vesicle.
Bulk export from a cell when an internal vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.
A double-membrane organelle containing most of a eukaryotic cell’s genetic material.
A double membrane with nuclear pores that regulates exchange between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
A nuclear region where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits begin assembly.
A membrane network bearing ribosomes that synthesizes and begins processing secreted or membrane proteins.
A ribosome-free membrane network involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage.
Stacks of membranes that modify, sort, and package proteins and lipids into vesicles.
An acidic, enzyme-filled organelle that digests macromolecules and worn cellular components.
An organelle that oxidizes selected molecules and breaks down hydrogen peroxide using catalase.
A double-membrane organelle where aerobic respiration produces most cellular ATP.
A photosynthetic organelle in plants and algae containing thylakoids, stroma, and its own DNA.
A cylindrical microtubule structure involved in organizing animal-cell spindle microtubules and basal bodies.
A small membrane-bound compartment that moves materials between organelles or the plasma membrane.
A large plant-cell compartment that stores solutes and helps maintain turgor pressure.
A dynamic network of protein filaments that supports cell shape, transport, division, and movement.
Interconnected or vesicle-linked membranes that synthesize, modify, and transport cell products.
Separation of cellular processes into distinct regions, allowing specialized and independently regulated conditions.
Development of distinct cell structures and functions through regulated changes in gene activity.
An unspecialized cell able to self-renew and produce one or more differentiated cell types.
Able to generate every cell type of an organism, including extraembryonic tissues.
Able to generate nearly any body cell type but not an entire organism with supporting tissues.
Able to generate several related cell types within a particular tissue or lineage.
A size relationship that generally decreases as a cell grows, limiting exchange across its boundary.
A red blood cell specialized for gas transport by its biconcave shape and high hemoglobin content.
A motile male gamete specialized to deliver a haploid nucleus to an egg.
A developing female germ cell that can mature into an ovum.
An excitable cell specialized to receive, process, and transmit electrical and chemical signals.
A long multinucleate cell packed with contractile myofibrils for voluntary movement.
A chloroplast-rich leaf cell specialized for light absorption and photosynthesis.
A root epidermal cell with a long projection that increases mineral-ion and water uptake.
A lignified dead cell joined end-to-end to conduct water and provide support.
A living phloem cell that conducts assimilates through perforated end walls with companion-cell support.
Movement of respiratory gases between an organism and its environment across a specialized surface.
Bulk movement of air or water that renews the medium at a respiratory surface.
A difference in one gas’s pressure that drives its net diffusion.
A microscopic lung air sac providing a thin, moist surface closely associated with capillaries.
A thin alveolar epithelial cell forming most of the surface across which gases diffuse.
An alveolar epithelial cell that secretes surfactant and can replace damaged alveolar cells.
A phospholipid-rich secretion that reduces alveolar surface tension and helps prevent collapse.
A dome-shaped skeletal muscle whose contraction increases thoracic volume during inhalation.
The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in one normal resting breath.
The greatest volume exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation.
The number of ventilation cycles per unit time, commonly measured as breaths per minute.
A slender gill projection bearing many lamellae and supporting blood vessels.
A thin plate on a gill filament that provides a large surface for aquatic gas exchange.
Opposite flow of blood and water that maintains an oxygen gradient across an entire gill surface.
A regulated epidermal pore through which carbon dioxide, oxygen, and water vapor move in plants.
One of a pair of specialized epidermal cells that controls the opening of a stoma.
Collective movement of a fluid and its dissolved substances down a pressure gradient.
A transport system in which blood remains within vessels separate from interstitial fluid.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart under relatively high pressure.
A blood vessel that carries blood toward the heart and commonly contains valves.
A microscopic, thin-walled vessel where materials exchange between blood and tissues.
The force per unit area exerted by circulating blood on vessel walls.
The repeating sequence of atrial and ventricular contraction and relaxation during one heartbeat.
The phase of a heart chamber’s cycle in which its muscle contracts.
The phase of a heart chamber’s cycle in which its muscle relaxes and the chamber fills.
A one-way valve between an atrium and ventricle that prevents backflow into the atrium.
A one-way valve at a ventricular outlet that prevents arterial blood returning to the ventricle.
The volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute, equal to heart rate times stroke volume.
An iron-containing tetrameric protein in red blood cells that reversibly binds oxygen.
Plant vascular tissue that conducts water and mineral ions and provides mechanical support.
Loss of water vapor from a plant, mainly by evaporation and diffusion through stomata.
The explanation that transpiration-generated tension pulls a cohesive water column upward through xylem.
Living vascular tissue that transports sucrose and other assimilates between plant sources and sinks.
Pressure-driven transport of organic assimilates through phloem sieve tubes.
A plant region that releases more assimilate into phloem than it consumes or stores.
A plant region that removes assimilate from phloem for use or storage.

sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

terms.definition: Striated muscle attached to the skeleton and generally controlled voluntarily.
A contractile bundle within a muscle fiber composed of repeating sarcomeres.
The repeating contractile unit of a myofibril between two Z discs.
The main protein of thin filaments, bearing sites that interact with myosin heads.
A motor protein whose heads bind actin and use ATP to generate force.
A filament protein that covers myosin-binding sites on actin when skeletal muscle is relaxed.
A regulatory protein complex that binds calcium and shifts tropomyosin away from actin’s binding sites.
Contraction by movement of thin filaments past thick filaments, shortening sarcomeres without shortening either filament.
A temporary attachment between a myosin head and an actin filament during contraction.
The pivot of an actin-bound myosin head that pulls the thin filament toward the sarcomere center.
A nerve cell that transmits signals from the central nervous system to muscle fibers.
The chemical synapse between a motor neuron terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber.
The neurotransmitter released by motor neurons to depolarize skeletal muscle fibers.
A specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium in muscle fibers.
Two muscles that move a joint in opposite directions because one contracts as the other relaxes.
An inherited feature that increases reproductive success in a particular environment.
A reversible physiological adjustment by an individual in response to an environmental change.
An inherited anatomical feature that improves performance or survival in a particular environment.
An inherited functional process that improves performance or survival under particular conditions.
An inherited pattern of action that improves survival or reproductive success.
The ability of one genotype to produce different phenotypes under different environmental conditions.
A plant adapted to habitats where liquid water is scarce.
A plant adapted to living partly or wholly in water.
A plant adapted to grow in a highly saline environment.
Control of body temperature through physiological or behavioral mechanisms.
An animal whose body temperature depends mainly on external heat sources.
An animal that maintains substantial body heat through internally generated metabolism.
Material or tissue that reduces heat transfer between an organism and its environment.
Opposite flow of warm and cool blood that conserves heat by maintaining a transfer gradient.
Control of water balance and solute concentrations in body fluids.
A species’ multidimensional role, resource use, and tolerated conditions within an ecosystem.
The full range of conditions and resources a species could use without biotic constraints.
The conditions and resources a species actually uses after biotic interactions restrict it.
The physical place or environment in which an organism lives.
Division of limited resources among competing species through differences in use, place, or time.
The prediction that species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely when a shared resource is limiting.
Competition between individuals of different species for a limiting resource.
Competition among members of the same species for a limiting resource.
An interaction in which one organism kills and consumes another organism.
A close interaction in which both participating species gain a net benefit.
An interaction in which one species benefits while the other is neither significantly helped nor harmed.
An interaction in which a parasite benefits while reducing the fitness of its host.
A non-living physical or chemical component of an environment.
A living component or biological interaction that affects an organism.
The span of an environmental variable within which an organism can survive and reproduce.
An environmental resource or condition whose scarcity or excess restricts distribution, abundance, or growth.
